card1.sentence: (3) After practice, <u>he</u> usually stays late to work on free kicks with the coach.
card1.why: Why: Marcus and Devon were both just introduced. "He" could mean either one — the reader has no way to know which. Fix: name him directly (e.g., "After practice, Devon usually stays late...").

card2.sentence: (2) <u>Her</u> mother studied music theory in college and now teaches private lessons on weekends.
card2.why: Why: "Her" could refer to either Priya's mother or Keisha's mother — there's no way to tell which. Same pattern as the first example: a pronoun shows up right after two people were named, with no single clear antecedent.

card3.sentence: "...worried that <u>it</u> might be damaged during the renovation." → "...worried that <ins>the vase</ins> might be damaged during the renovation."
card3.why: Why: Vague pronouns aren't just about people — "it" here could mean the vase OR the mirror, since both are singular objects named right before it. Naming the specific object removes the ambiguity.

card4.why: Why: "Them" has no stated antecedent — no noun in the sentence says who actually gets the equipment. Only the correct choice replaces the vague pronoun with a specific noun; the other choices all keep the unresolved "them."

card5.sentence: (2) ...swimming a mile in under seventeen minutes was considered remarkable, but <u>that</u> was drastically changed by Ledecky...
card5.why: Why: "That" doesn't point to any single named noun — it's trying to refer back to the whole idea that seventeen minutes was remarkable, which isn't a noun a pronoun can cleanly stand in for.

card6.sentence: (4) Grandma blends each smoothie until <u>they turn</u> smooth... → until <ins>it turns</ins> smooth, while all three grandchildren set the table for a cold<ins>,</ins> refreshing treat.
card6.why: Why: The antecedent is "each smoothie" — singular — so it needs "it turns," not "they turn." Separately, "cold" and "refreshing" are two independent adjectives both describing "treat," so they need a comma between them.

card7.sentence: (3) The preparation of Chicago-style pizza involves <u>a layer of cheese, and sauce, which is added</u> before the crust is baked in a deep pan. → a layer of cheese and sauce, which <ins>are added</ins> before the crust is baked in a deep pan.
card7.why: Why: The subject of "is added" is "a layer of cheese...and sauce" — a compound (two-part) subject, which is always plural, so it needs "are added." The stray comma after "cheese" also gets deleted since "a layer of cheese and sauce" is a simple pair, not a list.

card8.sentence: (4) ...scientists <u>used</u> powerful telescopes to study their composition and origin. → scientists <ins>use</ins> powerful telescopes to study their composition and origin.
card8.why: Why: The rest of the paragraph is present tense ("are," "causes," "can develop"), so "used" breaks that consistency — nothing in the sentence signals that this one action happened only in the past. It should be "use."

card9.sentence: (4) ...which removes more <u>sediment, and allow</u> the final cup to taste cleaner and lighter. → ...which removes more <ins>sediment and allows</ins> the final cup to taste cleaner and lighter.
card9.why: Why: The subject of "allow" is "which" (referring back to the paper filter removing sediment) — a singular idea, so it needs "allows." The comma before "and allow(s)" also gets deleted since it's joining two things the filter does, not two separate sentences.

card10.sentence: (4) ...a landmark that <u>becomes</u> a UNESCO World Heritage <u>Site,</u> after it was added to the list in 1996. → ...a landmark that <ins>became</ins> a UNESCO World Heritage <ins>Site</ins> after it was added to the list in 1996.
card10.why: Why: "Became" matches the past-tense context ("after it was added to the list in 1996") — "becomes" would wrongly suggest it's an ongoing, repeated event. And "Site" shouldn't have a comma before "after," since that's not where a new clause needs to be set off.

card11.sentence: (1) <u>Sorting donations, organizing shelves, and greeting visitors, the community food pantry is looking for volunteers...</u>
card11.why: Why: It's not the pantry that sorts donations and greets visitors — it's the volunteers. The opening phrase dangles because the noun right after the comma ("the community food pantry") isn't who's actually doing those actions.

card12.sentence: (3) <u>Her poems exploring themes of resilience and identity throughout American history.</u>
card12.why: Why: This is a fragment, not a complete sentence — "exploring" is a participle, not a real verb. It needs something like "explore" or "explored" to actually make the subject "her poems" do something.

card13.sentence: (1) There is considerable evidence that early trade networks were greatly influenced by how well merchants could navigate difficult mountain terrain, <u>such as the Silk Road traders crossing the Himalayas</u>.
card13.why: Why: "Such as the Silk Road traders crossing the Himalayas" is meant to give an example of "early trade networks," but as written it's placed right after "mountain terrain" — making it sound like the terrain is being exemplified, not the trade networks. A misplaced modifier needs to move next to the thing it actually describes.

card14.sentence: (2) <u>Launching a towering home run over the center-field wall, the crowd roared with excitement,</u> and her team secured the victory.
card14.why: Why: The crowd didn't launch the home run — Mia Alvarez did. Same dangling-modifier pattern as the other examples: check who's really doing the "-ing" action right after the comma.

card15.sentence: (1) <u>After finishing high school, the next four years of a nursing student's life are spent completing clinical rotations...</u>
card15.why: Why: It's the nursing student who finishes high school, not "the next four years." Another dangling opening modifier — the subject right after the comma should be the one doing the finishing.

card16.sentence: "<ins>Because</ins> Elena had practiced her violin piece for months, she performed the solo with confidence, <ins>and</ins> her performance earned a standing ovation from the audience."
card16.why: Why: All three ideas are a cause-and-effect chain (practice → confidence → ovation). "Because" correctly marks the cause; "and" just adds the final result. Wrong choices use "yet," "so...but" — words that imply contrast or a problem, which isn't what's happening here.

card17.sentence: "The years of intense training that young gymnasts need to dedicate in order to compete at an elite level <ins>is impossible without</ins> the guidance and support of experienced coaches."
card17.why: Why: Sentence 1 says gymnasts need to dedicate years of training; sentence 2 adds that this is only possible with coaches' support. Option C keeps both main ideas intact by directly linking them with "is impossible without" — the same relationship the original two sentences state. The other choices shift the emphasis (A, B make it sound like two loosely related facts) or restructure the idea in a way that changes what's being said (D).

card18.sentence: "The city's new transit authority plans to build a light-rail line downtown; <ins>afterwards,</ins> this rail line will serve as a key connector for future suburban extensions."
card18.why: Why: This is a sequence in time (light-rail line first, connector role after), not a contrast — "afterwards" correctly marks that order. "Although/but" choices would wrongly imply the two ideas conflict with each other.

card19.sentence: "Satellite missions studying Saturn, <ins>which allow scientists to collect data about the planet's rings and moons,</ins> have been ongoing since 1997."
card19.why: Why: Sentence 2 is just extra description of "satellite missions," so it folds into sentence 1 as a "which" clause rather than being tacked on with "and" or turned into a false cause/contrast.

card20.sentence: "Scientists now believe that Saturn may have more than one hundred and forty-five moons, <ins>including one named Titan, which has</ins> a dense atmosphere and liquid methane lakes."
card20.why: Why: Sentence 1 is the main idea; sentences 2–3 are both just further detail about one specific moon, so "including...which" nests them both as description rather than giving them equal weight with "and."

card21.sentence: "...opened as part of a growing wave of hands-on science <u>museums, the</u> museum is already..." → "...hands-on science <ins>museums; the</ins> museum is already..."
card21.why: Why: "The museum opened..." and "the museum is already..." are both complete sentences on their own — a plain comma can't join two complete sentences, so it needs a semicolon. (The other three underlined spots are correctly punctuated — they're just decoys.)

card22.sentence: "The <u>curious</u> determined astronomer Dr. Lena Park became..." → "The <ins>curious,</ins> determined astronomer Dr. Lena Park became..."
card22.why: Why: "Curious" and "determined" are two separate, equal adjectives both describing "astronomer" ("curious AND determined astronomer" works), so they need a comma between them.

card23.sentence: "Many historians agree that Ada Lovelace, <u>a pioneering mathematician</u> is nearly as influential..." → "...Ada Lovelace, <ins>a pioneering mathematician,</ins> is nearly as influential..."
card23.why: Why: "A pioneering mathematician" is nonessential extra information about Ada Lovelace, so it needs a comma on BOTH sides to be properly set off — the sentence only has the opening comma, not the closing one.

card24.sentence: "...is limited <u>sunlight,</u> another issue that plagues..." → "...is limited <ins>sunlight; another</ins> issue that plagues these gardeners is the high cost of raised garden beds."
card24.why: Why: "...is limited sunlight" and "another issue...is the high cost..." are each a complete sentence on their own — a plain comma can't join two complete sentences, so it needs to become a semicolon.

card25.sentence: "Riverdale needed increased <u>funding, for</u> schools, <u>and subsequently</u> the town built..." → "Riverdale needed increased <ins>funding for</ins> schools, <ins>and, subsequently,</ins> the town built..."
card25.why: Why: "Funding for schools" is one tight phrase that shouldn't be split by a comma; "subsequently" is an inserted transition word that needs its own commas on both sides, not a bare "and subsequently."

card26.sentence: "Diego wandered the farmers market looking for <u>some fresh things for his breakfast</u>." → "...looking for <ins>ripe tomatoes and a loaf of sourdough</ins>."
card26.why: Why: The rest of the paragraph already tells us exactly what he bought — tomatoes and sourdough. The precise revision uses those specific items instead of "some fresh things."

card27.sentence: "The Golden Gate Bridge was such a big distance across the water and took a really long time to finish..." → "The Golden Gate Bridge required <ins>a 1.7-mile span across the strait and four years of construction</ins>..."
card27.why: Why: "Big distance" and "really long time" are vague; the best choice swaps in the actual measurable facts (1.7 miles, four years, the strait) rather than just rephrasing the vagueness with fancier synonyms.

card28.sentence: "...the local reporter calmly and clearly <u>explained to all of the people who were reading the morning paper what was happening</u>." → "...the local reporter calmly and clearly <ins>reported on the dispute for the morning paper</ins>."
card28.why: Why: "All of the people who were reading the morning paper" is a wordy way of just saying "for the morning paper," and "what was happening" is replaced with the specific event already named earlier in the sentence: "the dispute."

card29.sentence: "...because the curved stone seating <u>sends the sound through the environment</u>." → "...because the curved stone seating <ins>directs the sound waves to move along the curve of the seating</ins>."
card29.why: Why: "Send...through the environment" is vague — it doesn't say how. The fix names the actual mechanism already implied by "curved stone seating": sound waves following the curve.

card30.sentence: "Cameron made his math grade better by doing extra work." → "Cameron <ins>improved</ins> his math grade by <ins>completing all available extra-credit projects</ins>."
card30.why: Why: C uses the most precise, concise verb ("improved" instead of the vague "made better") and the clearest specific action ("completing all available extra-credit projects") without extra padding. B has an awkward "his doing" construction and a vague "not as low"; A and D are specific but wordier than they need to be.

card31.sentence: (1) A skilled surgeon, the doctor, <u>who treats patients,</u> is known throughout the hospital for steady hands and careful technique.
card31.why: Why: "Who treats patients" is redundant — the sentence already says "doctor" and "surgeon," both of which already mean someone who treats patients. The clause doesn't add any new information, it just restates what's already known.

card32.sentence: (1) The committee reviewed <u>each and every</u> application before making a final decision. → The committee reviewed <ins>every</ins> application before making a final decision.
card32.why: Why: "Each" and "every" mean the same thing here — pairing them doesn't add emphasis, it just says the same word twice. One or the other is enough.

card33.sentence: (2) <u>Every single one of</u> the participants completed the entire survey... → <ins>All of</ins> the participants completed the entire survey...
card33.why: Why: "Every," "single," and "one" are all doing the same job of emphasizing totality — stacking all three doesn't add meaning, it just repeats it. "All of the participants" or "Every participant" says the exact same thing in fewer words.

card34.sentence: (1) The weather service issued an <u>advance warning</u> before the storm made landfall... → The weather service issued <ins>a warning</ins> before the storm made landfall...
card34.why: Why: "Advance warning" is redundant — a warning is, by definition, something given in advance. It could simply say "a warning."

card35.sentence: (1) <u>Due to the fact that</u> ticket sales exceeded expectations, the concert venue added a second show. → <ins>Because</ins> ticket sales exceeded expectations, the concert venue added a second show.
card35.why: Why: "Due to the fact that" is a wordy way of saying "because" — it takes five words to do the job of one, without adding any meaning.

card36.sentence: "...<u>it's</u> vibrant colors still catch the eye..." → "...<ins>its</ins> vibrant colors still catch the eye..."
card36.why: Why: "It's" always means "it is" — try the substitution: "it is vibrant colors" doesn't make sense, so this needs the possessive "its" (no apostrophe).

card37.sentence: "...which had not been <u>rang</u> since the school's founding..." → "...which had not been <ins>rung</ins> since the school's founding..."
card37.why: Why: After "had been" (passive voice), irregular verbs need their participle form — "rung," not the simple past "rang." You'd say "the bell rang," but "the bell had been rung."

card38.sentence: "The volunteers <u>that</u> organized the fundraiser..." → "The volunteers <ins>who</ins> organized the fundraiser..."
card38.why: Why: "Volunteers" are people — "who" should be used for people, while "that" is reserved for things, animals, or groups treated as a single unit.

card39.sentence: "Between Maya and Jade, Maya is the <u>best</u> sprinter..." → "...Maya is the <ins>better</ins> sprinter..."
card39.why: Why: Only two people are being compared ("Between Maya and Jade"), so this needs the comparative "better," not the superlative "best" — "best" is reserved for comparing three or more.

card40.sentence: (4) ...when translating between two <u>close</u> related languages... → ...when translating between two <ins>closely</ins> related languages...
card40.why: Why: The word modifying "related" (an adjective here) needs to be an adverb — "closely," not the adjective "close." You can't use an adjective to describe another adjective.
